## Statement

Assume the normal specialization of [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] with
parameter space $\Theta=\mathbb R$ and hyperparameter space
$H=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau^2>0$.
Conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let the
group parameters be independent with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Let the
observed group summaries be conditionally independent with
$\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,s_j^2)$, where each known $s_j^2>0$. In this normal specialization, the supplied
likelihood-density version is the canonical normal density at every parameter
and observation value:
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
Then, conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2,\bar Y_1=\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_m=\bar y_m)$,
the $\theta_j$ are independent and
$$\theta_j\sim N(\hat\theta_j,V_j),\qquad\hat\theta_j=\frac{\bar y_j/s_j^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2},\qquad V_j=\left(1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1}.$$
If $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is unknown with a proper hyperprior supported on
$\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, let $P_y$ be the full posterior kernel from
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]] and,
on each positive finite evidence fiber, define its hyperparameter marginal on
Borel $C\subseteq H$ by $\Pi_y(C):=P_y(C\times\mathbb R^m)$. The posterior law of
$\theta_j$ is the mixture of these conditional normal laws over $\Pi_y$;
replacing $\mu,\tau^2$ by point estimates is not this posterior. No normalized
hyperparameter posterior is asserted on a zero or infinite evidence fiber.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normal hierarchical model, known positive sampling variances $s_j^2$, positive conditional prior variance $\tau^2$, and the stated observed group summaries.

[F1] Conditional on the hyperparameters, the model uses the normal prior $N(\mu,\tau^2)$ and group observation kernels with the canonical normal density factors $f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-\theta)^2/(2s_j^2))$ specified pointwise in the Statement; these factors are jointly measurable, and distinct groups factor under the specified product kernels. [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]

[F2] The finite product observation kernel has its specified product density. [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]]

[F3] On a positive finite evidence fiber, the posterior of the full latent tuple is the normalized joint likelihood density. [[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]]

[F4] Tonelli passes nonnegative integrals through the finite product likelihood and the hyperparameter integral. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F5] For a proper normal prior $N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ and $n\ge1$ IID observations from $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known positive variance, the evidence is finite positive and the posterior has precision $\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2}$ and precision-weighted mean. [[thm-normal-normal-conjugate-update]]

[F6] Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system are equal when that pi-system has an increasing finite-measure exhaustion. [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]]

[F7] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a finite probability kernel gives a measurable function of its source parameter. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F8] Sections and coordinate projections in finite product measurable spaces are measurable, and measurable rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. [[thm-sections-of-product-measurable-functions-are-measurable]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F9] Finite products of probability kernels with a common source are probability kernels and satisfy the product rectangle formula. [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]

[A1] AC is assumed for the library normal-law and conditional-expectation-class conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] $\tau^2>0$ and all $s_j^2>0$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** specialize the BCS-03 Normal–Normal update to each group, factor the finite conditional posterior, and integrate over the hyperparameter posterior.

**Given:** The stated fixed hyperparameters, group summaries, and variances.

1.1 Fix a group $j$ and specialize [F5] to one observation: identify its parameter with $\theta_j$, set $\mu_0=\mu$, $\tau_0^2=\tau^2$, $n=1$, $y_1=\bar y_j$, and $\sigma^2=s_j^2$. The model and pointwise density specification in [F1] supply this normal prior and the canonical normal likelihood density used by [F5], while [A1] and [A2] verify the choice and positive-variance hypotheses of [F5]. The theorem gives a finite positive group evidence and posterior variance $V_j=(1/\tau^2+1/s_j^2)^{-1}$ and mean $\hat\theta_j=V_j(\mu/\tau^2+\bar y_j/s_j^2)$, as stated. [A1, A2, F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 For each group put $\mu_j(A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$ and let $m_j=\mu_j(\mathbb R)>0$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mu_j/m_j=Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$. Apply [F3] to the hierarchy with the proper point-mass hyperprior at the fixed $(\mu,\tau^2)$. Its latent prior on $\mathbb R^m$ is the product of the group priors by [F1], and its likelihood density is $\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,\bar y_j)$ by [F2]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] shows that the normalized posterior assigns each measurable rectangle $\prod_j A_j$ mass $\prod_j\mu_j(A_j)/\prod_jm_j=\prod_jQ_j(A_j)$, the rectangle mass of $\bigotimes_jQ_j$ by [F9]. By [F8], rectangles form a generating pi-system. Both are probability measures agreeing on it; the constant exhaustion by the full space has common finite mass one, so [F6] makes them equal. This proves conditional independence and the displayed formula for every group. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Now suppose $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is random with a proper hyperprior supported on $H$. For fixed observed summaries, put $M_j((\mu,\tau^2),A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$. The factor $f_j(\cdot,\bar y_j)$ is measurable by the section fact [F8]; composing it with the parameter-coordinate projection shows that $(\eta,\theta)\mapsto1_A(\theta)f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)$ is product-measurable. Since $G_\eta=N(\mu,\tau^2)$ is a probability kernel, [F7] makes $M_j(\cdot,A)$ measurable. Hence $m_j=M_j(\cdot,\mathbb R)$ and $Q_j(A)=M_j(\cdot,A)/m_j$ are measurable, with $m_j>0$ by step 1.1. Repeated Tonelli [F4] and the full-posterior formula [F3] give, for measurable $C\subseteq H$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\mathbb R$, $P_y(C\times\prod_jA_j)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jM_j((\mu,\tau^2),A_j)\,\Pi(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. Taking every $A_j=\mathbb R$ shows $\Pi_y(C)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_C\prod_jm_j\,d\Pi$. Taking only $A_j=A$ and all other sets equal to $\mathbb R$ therefore gives $P_y(\theta_j\in A)=\int_HQ_j(A)\,\Pi_y(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$, so the group posterior is its conditional normal law averaged over the full hyperparameter posterior, rather than a point estimate. [F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$ be the data space and
$\mathcal Y_+=\{y\in\mathcal Y:0<Z(y)<\infty\}$ its measurable subset of
positive finite evidence fibers. Write $P_y$ for the full latent probability
kernel supplied by
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]], and
set $\Lambda_y:=P_y$ for every $y\in\mathcal Y$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ this is
the normalized joint posterior; off $\mathcal Y_+$ it is the prior filler
$P_0$, so no likelihood quotient is formed there. For an already observed
group $j$, its **current-group posterior predictive law** for a future
observation with the same conditional observation kernel is
$$Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)=\int_\Xi K_j(\theta_j,A)\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$

For a new group, specify a probability kernel $K_{\mathrm{new}}$ from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a future observation space
$(\widetilde{\mathcal Y},\widetilde{\mathcal A})$. Its **new-group posterior
predictive law** is
$$Q^{\mathrm{new}}_y(A)=\int_\Xi\left[\int_\Theta K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,A)\,G_\eta(d\theta)\right]\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
For $y\in\mathcal Y_+$, if $\Lambda_y^\eta$ denotes the hyperparameter
marginal of $\Lambda_y$, the joint posterior law of
$(\eta,\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$ used here is
$\Lambda_y^\eta(d\eta)G_\eta(d\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$. Thus the new-group
prediction first draws a new latent parameter from $G_\eta$ and then draws its
observation from $K_{\mathrm{new}}$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ both formulas average
over the joint posterior and retain uncertainty about unknown hyperparameters.
On exceptional fibers they reduce to prior-predictive laws because
$\Lambda_y=P_0$.

## Statement

Under [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]], the current-group and new-group
predictive assignments of
[[def-current-and-new-group-posterior-predictive-laws]] are probability
kernels on the full data space $\mathcal Y$. On every positive finite evidence
fiber they are the stated posterior-predictive laws. On zero or infinite
evidence fibers, the posterior kernel uses its prior filler, so the predictions
are the corresponding prior-predictive laws. When a future current-group
observation is drawn from $K_j$ conditional on the latent tuple, or a future
new-group parameter is first drawn from $G_\eta$ and then observed from
$K_{\mathrm{new}}$, these kernels are conditional laws of the future
observations given the observed data. This is a posterior-predictive statement
under the specified model, not a frequentist coverage claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A proper hierarchical model, its posterior kernel on $\mathcal Y_+$, and the future observation kernels specified in the predictive definition.

[F1] For every $y\in\mathcal Y$, $P_y$ is a probability measure and conditional law of the latent tuple; it is the normalized posterior on positive finite evidence fibers and equals $P_0$ on zero or infinite evidence fibers. The evidence-positive set is measurable and has prior-predictive probability one. [[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]]

[F2] $G_\eta$, each current-group $K_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$, and $K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,\cdot)$ are probability kernels. [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]], [[def-current-and-new-group-posterior-predictive-laws]]

[F3] Integrating a nonnegative measurable function against a kernel gives a measurable function. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]

[F4] Increasing nonnegative limits pass through integrals. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F5] Integrating a nonnegative measurable function against a regular conditional law gives the conditional integral on every conditioning event. [[thm-conditional-integration-through-a-regular-conditional-law]]

[F6] A proper prior and a probability model kernel define a joint probability law with the iterated-integral identity. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

[F7] The finite product of probability kernels with a common source is a probability kernel. [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** verify probability-kernel mixture properties, then check the conditional-event identity for a future draw.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a current group $j$ and $y\in\mathcal Y$. For each measurable future-event set $A$, the formula $Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)=\int K_j(\theta_j,A)\,P_y(d\xi)$ gives zero on $A=\varnothing$ and one on the full observation space by [F1] and [F2]. If $(A_k)_{k\ge0}$ are disjoint, then $K_j(\theta_j,\bigcup_kA_k)=\lim_N\sum_{k\le N}K_j(\theta_j,A_k)$; [F4] passes this increasing limit through the $P_y$ integral and gives countable additivity. The integrand is measurable in $\xi$ by the kernel definition and coordinate projection, so [F3] makes $y\mapsto Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)$ measurable against the posterior kernel $y\mapsto P_y$. Thus each $Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_j$ is a probability kernel on $\mathcal Y$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

1.2 For a new group, define $R_\eta(A)=\int K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,A)G_\eta(d\theta)$. The empty-set and whole-space evaluations are zero and one. For disjoint $(A_k)$, countable additivity of each $K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,\cdot)$ and [F4] pass the increasing partial sums through the $G_\eta$ integral; hence $R_\eta$ is a probability measure. [F3] makes $\eta\mapsto R_\eta(A)$ measurable, so $R$ is a probability kernel. Mixing $R_\eta(A)$ over $P_y$ through the measurable coordinate $\eta$ and repeating the countable-additivity argument shows that $Q^{\mathrm{new}}_y(A)$ is a probability measure and [F3] makes its evaluations measurable in $y$. Its integral through the marginal $P_y^\eta$ is the same iterated-kernel law. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 For either prediction let $H(\xi,A)$ be its conditional future-event probability given the latent tuple: $K_j(\theta_j,A)$ for a current group, or $R_\eta(A)$ for a new group. Steps 1.1–1.2 make $H$ a probability kernel. By [F7], the product of the observation kernel and this future kernel is a probability kernel from $\Xi$ to the product of data and future-observation spaces; applying [F6] with prior $P_0$ gives a joint probability law on $(\xi,Y,\widetilde Y)$. Because every section of $H$ has total mass one, marginalizing out $\widetilde Y$ leaves the original joint law of $(\xi,Y)$, so [F1] still supplies its posterior conditional law $P_y$. For data event $B$ and future event $A$, the triple law gives $P(Y\in B,\widetilde Y\in A)=E[1_{\{Y\in B\}}H(\xi,A)]$. Applying the event identity in [F5] to $H(\xi,A)$ turns the right side into $\int_B\int H(\xi,A)\,P_y(d\xi)\,P_Y(dy)=\int_B Q_y(A)\,P_Y(dy)$. This verifies the conditional-event identity for every data event $B$ and proves that both full-data kernels are the conditional laws of the future observations. Since $P_y=P_0$ off $\mathcal Y_+$, their exceptional-fiber predictions are the prior-predictive laws. [F1, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Take one group with $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$ and $Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$, where $t=\tau^2>0$. Observe $y=0$, but replace the proper hyperprior in [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] by the improper measure $\Pi(dt)=t^{-1}dt$ on $(0,\infty)$. Its evidence-weighted density is not integrable, so it cannot be normalized to a posterior probability. This is a warning example outside the proper-hyperprior hypotheses of the hierarchical posterior theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-group normal model in the Example, observation $y=0$, and the improper hyperparameter density $1/t$ on $(0,\infty)$.

[F1] For $a\in\mathbb R$ and $v>0$, the $N(a,v)$ density is $(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-a)^2/(2v)}$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F2] The standard normal density has Lebesgue integral one. [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]]

[F3] For a sigma-finite prior measure, the evidence is the integral of the likelihood section, and a finite positive scaling of the likelihood-weighted measure is a probability exactly when the evidence is finite and positive. [[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]], [[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]]

[A1] AC is assumed for the library normal-law convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] The hyperprior measure is $\Pi(dt)=t^{-1}dt$ on $(0,\infty)$.

## Verification

**Given:** The model, observation, and improper hyperprior in the Example.

1.1 The prior is sigma-finite: the sets $E_n=[1/n,n]$ increase to $(0,\infty)$ and $\Pi(E_n)=\int_{1/n}^n dt/t=2\log n<\infty$. Integrating out $\theta$ gives the evidence at fixed $t$, $m(0\mid t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta^2/(2t)}}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\frac{e^{-\theta^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,d\theta=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)}}$. Indeed, the exponent is $-(1+t^{-1})\theta^2/2$; the substitution $z=\sqrt{1+t^{-1}}\,\theta$ reduces the integral to the unit normal integral [F2]. It is positive and finite for every $t>0$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The evidence-weighted density of $t$ is $q(t)=1/(t\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)})$ by [A2] and step 1.1. For each $k\ge0$, let $I_k=(2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k})$. On $I_k\subset(0,1)$, $q(t)\ge1/(t\sqrt{4\pi})$ and $1/t\ge2^k$, while the interval has length $2^{-(k+1)}$. Hence $\int_{I_k}q(t)\,dt\ge1/(2\sqrt{4\pi})$, uniformly in $k$. The intervals are disjoint, so summing their lower bounds shows $\int_0^1q(t)\,dt=\infty$. By [F3], no finite positive scaling makes this likelihood-weighted measure a posterior probability. [A2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let the hyperparameter be $t=\tau^2\in\{1,4\}$ with prior probability
$1/2$ at each value. There is one group, $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$, and
$Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$. Observe $y=0$. Specify the likelihood-density version pointwise by
$$f(\theta,y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-\theta)^2/2)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
The full posterior for $\theta$
is a mixture of the two conditional normal posteriors. Plugging in the
posterior mode of $t$ instead yields just one component, which is not the full
posterior.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A proper two-point hyperprior on $t\in\{1,4\}$, one group parameter $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$, an observation kernel $Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$, and observed value $y=0$.

[F1] The hierarchy's prior and observation kernels define the joint latent-data model. [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]

[F3] A proper prior probability and parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel constitute a Bayesian model. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]].

[F4] Evidence is the prior integral of the joint likelihood section; the normalized quotient is introduced only on finite positive evidence. [[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]].

## Definition

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

## Remarks

The product-kernel assumption is part of this model. An arbitrary finitely
exchangeable law need not be a mixture of iid laws; no finite de Finetti theorem
is claimed here. When $\eta$ is unknown, the joint posterior retains its
uncertainty and induces dependence between group parameters after $\eta$ is
integrated out.

## Statement

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A proper hyperprior, finite product group and observation kernels, and their specified jointly measurable likelihood densities.

[F1] The finite-group model defines a proper latent prior $P_0$ and the product observation kernel with likelihood section $L_y$. [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]

[F2] The finite product of the group observation kernels has jointly measurable product density $L(\xi,y)=\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$ relative to the sigma-finite product measure $\nu$. [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]]

[F3] A proper prior and probability model kernel define a joint probability law with the corresponding iterated-integral identity. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

[F4] For a proper prior and a dominated probability kernel with a specified jointly measurable density, the posterior kernel is the normalized density on $0<m(y)<\infty$ fibers and uses the prior as filler on zero or infinite normalizer fibers. [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** identify the finite product likelihood density and apply the dominated-kernel Bayes formula.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1] and [F3], the latent prior $P_0$ is a probability measure and the model kernel gives a joint probability law for the latent tuple and the observations. By [F2], that observation kernel is dominated by the sigma-finite product measure $\nu$ with the specified jointly measurable density $L(\xi,y)=\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$. Thus all hypotheses of [F4] apply with prior $P_0$ and likelihood density $L$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 The resulting evidence is $m(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)P_0(d\xi)=Z(y)$. On every fiber with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, [F4] gives the probability measure $P_y(A)=Z(y)^{-1}\int_A L_y\,dP_0$ and the conditional-event identities. On fibers with zero or infinite evidence [F4] uses the probability filler $P_0$, so its kernel remains a regular conditional distribution there without dividing by zero or infinity. The same theorem says these filled fibers have prior-predictive measure zero. [F4, step 1.1] ∎

Fix a finite group count $m\ge1$, a standard Borel hyperparameter space
$(H,\mathcal H)$, and a standard Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$.
Let $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(H,\mathcal H)$ and let
$$G:H\times\mathcal T\to[0,1]$$
be a probability kernel. For each $j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let
$(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ be a measurable observation space, let $\nu_j$
be a sigma-finite measure on it, and let $K_j$ be a probability kernel from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathcal Y_j,\mathcal A_j)$ with a specified
jointly measurable density $f_j:\Theta\times\mathcal Y_j\to[0,\infty]$:
$$K_j(\theta,B)=\int_B f_j(\theta,y_j)\,\nu_j(dy_j)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$

The **finite-group hierarchical model** is the following specified kernel
construction. First draw $\eta\sim\Pi$. Conditional on $\eta$, draw
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m$ from the finite product kernel
$$G_\eta^{\otimes m}(d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j).$$
Thus the group parameters are conditionally independent and have the same
conditional law $G_\eta$. Conditional on the parameter tuple, draw the group
observations from the product kernel $\bigotimes_{j=1}^mK_j(\theta_j,\cdot)$.
The product-kernel laws are probability kernels by
[[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]. For each fixed $\eta$, the
coordinate maps under $G_\eta^{\otimes m}$ are independent random elements,
so their joint law is the finite product law
([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]).

Put $\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$ with its finite product sigma-algebra. The proper
latent prior $P_0$ on $\Xi$ is
$$P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m)=\Pi(d\eta)\prod_{j=1}^mG_\eta(d\theta_j),$$
well-defined by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. For
$\xi=(\eta,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m)\in\Xi$, lift each observation kernel
to the common source $\Xi$ by
$$M_j(\xi,B)=K_j(\theta_j,B)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A_j).$$
The coordinate projection $\xi\mapsto\theta_j$ is measurable, so the kernel
definition shows that each $M_j$ is a probability kernel. Its specified
jointly measurable density is $(\xi,y_j)\mapsto f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$, by
composition with the same measurable coordinate projection. Let
$\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$,
$\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\nu_j$, and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$. The observation
kernel from $\Xi$ has jointly measurable density
$$L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)=\prod_{j=1}^m f_j(\theta_j,y_j)$$
with respect to $\nu$, by [[lem-finite-products-of-dominated-kernels-have-product-density]].
Its **evidence** is the possibly extended nonnegative number
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\eta,\theta_1\cdots\theta_m)\,P_0(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
The normalized likelihood measure is called a pointwise joint posterior on a
fiber only when $0<Z(y)<\infty$; no quotient is formed at zero or infinite
evidence.

For each group, $\theta\mapsto K_j(\theta,\cdot)$ is a parametric statistical
model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]], with its
parameter-measurable kernel representation as in
[[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]. Here
“conditionally independent given $\eta$” is shorthand for the explicit
finite product-kernel specification above. The library's random-element
conditional-independence terminology is defined in
[[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]; its
conditional-expectation-class convention assumes AC. The finite
product-kernel definition here does not use that class convention or any
choice axiom.

Assume the finite-group hierarchical model of
[[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]]. Write $P_0$ for its proper prior on
$\Xi=H\times\Theta^m$, let $L_y(\xi)$ be its specified product likelihood
density with respect to the finite product measure $\nu$, and define
$$Z(y)=\int_\Xi L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi).$$
For every observation $y$ with $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the measure
$$P_y(A)=\frac{\int_A L_y(\xi)\,P_0(d\xi)}{Z(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal T^{\otimes m})$$
is the joint posterior law of the latent tuple. Defining $P_y=P_0$ when
$Z(y)=0$ or $Z(y)=\infty$ gives a regular conditional distribution under the
prior-predictive law; no quotient is formed on either exceptional fiber.

Assume the normal specialization of [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] with
parameter space $\Theta=\mathbb R$ and hyperparameter space
$H=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau^2>0$.
Conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let the
group parameters be independent with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Let the
observed group summaries be conditionally independent with
$\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,s_j^2)$, where each known $s_j^2>0$. In this normal specialization, the supplied
likelihood-density version is the canonical normal density at every parameter
and observation value:
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
Then, conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2,\bar Y_1=\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_m=\bar y_m)$,
the $\theta_j$ are independent and
$$\theta_j\sim N(\hat\theta_j,V_j),\qquad\hat\theta_j=\frac{\bar y_j/s_j^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2},\qquad V_j=\left(1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1}.$$
If $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is unknown with a proper hyperprior supported on
$\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, let $P_y$ be the full posterior kernel from
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]] and,
on each positive finite evidence fiber, define its hyperparameter marginal on
Borel $C\subseteq H$ by $\Pi_y(C):=P_y(C\times\mathbb R^m)$. The posterior law of
$\theta_j$ is the mixture of these conditional normal laws over $\Pi_y$;
replacing $\mu,\tau^2$ by point estimates is not this posterior. No normalized
hyperparameter posterior is asserted on a zero or infinite evidence fiber.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The specified model supplies the prior and sampling kernels [F1]; their densities are given by [F4]. For fixed $t>0$, multiply the two densities and integrate over $\theta$. The integrand is $(2\pi\sqrt t)^{-1}\exp(-(1+t^{-1})\theta^2/2)$. Substituting $z=\sqrt{1+t^{-1}}\,\theta$ and using [F5] for the unit normal integral gives the marginal evidence $m_t(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi(1+t)}$, which is positive and finite for $t=1,4$.

The two prior masses are equal, so [F2] gives posterior odds $P(t=1\mid y=0)/P(t=4\mid y=0)=m_1(0)/m_4(0)=\sqrt{5/2}>1$. Thus the posterior mode is $t=1$, and the posterior weights $w=P(t=1\mid y=0)$ and $1-w$ are both strictly between zero and one.
By [F3], $\theta\mid t=1,y=0\sim N(0,1/2)$ and $\theta\mid t=4,y=0\sim N(0,4/5)$. The full posterior is their mixture with weights $w$ and $1-w$, so its second moment is $w/2+(1-w)4/5>1/2$.

Plugging in the posterior mode $t=1$ gives only $N(0,1/2)$, whose second moment is $1/2$. This differs from the full posterior's second moment in step 3.1, so the plug-in posterior is not the full posterior mixture.

derivations.claim: Set $a_j=\tau^2/(\tau^2+s_j^2)$. Algebra in [F1] gives $\hat\theta_j=a_j\bar y_j+(1-a_j)\mu$ and $V_j=\tau^2s_j^2/(\tau^2+s_j^2)$. Since both variances are positive, $0<a_j<1$, so for finite positive $\tau^2$ the group mean uses both its own data and the population mean.

item.title: Integrating hyperparameter uncertainty versus plugging in
item.statement:
Let the hyperparameter be $t=\tau^2\in\{1,4\}$ with prior probability
$1/2$ at each value. There is one group, $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$, and
$Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$. Observe $y=0$. Specify the likelihood-density version pointwise by
$$f(\theta,y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-\theta)^2/2)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
The full posterior for $\theta$
is a mixture of the two conditional normal posteriors. Plugging in the
posterior mode of $t$ instead yields just one component, which is not the full
posterior.

item.title: Complete, partial, and no-pooling limits in the normal hierarchy
item.statement:
In the known-variance normal hierarchy, fix $\mu$, an observed group summary
$\bar y_j$, and $s_j^2>0$. Specify the likelihood-density version pointwise by
$$f_j(\theta,y)=(2\pi s_j^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{2s_j^2}\right)\qquad(\theta,y\in\mathbb R).$$
For finite $\tau^2>0$, the posterior mean is a
strictly weighted average of $\bar y_j$ and $\mu$. As $\tau^2\downarrow0$ it
approaches complete pooling at $\mu$; at the boundary $\tau^2=0$, the prior
itself forces $\theta_j=\mu$. As $\tau^2\to\infty$, the posterior mean and
variance approach the group-only values $\bar y_j$ and $s_j^2$, the
no-pooling limit. The value $\tau^2=\infty$ is not an admissible proper prior.
item.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the library normal-law definition used for the degenerate boundary; the weight and limit calculations are choice-free.
